A B S T R A C T
In this paper, we propose two new approaches for acoustic emission (AE) source localization in
highly anisotropic plates without the need for apriori knowledge of their material properties or
the orientation of the axes of symmetry. These approaches, namely the equation error approach
(EEA) and Bayesian inference approach (BIA), offer significant improvements over the latest
wavefront shape-based techniques reported in the literature. In particular, the EEA requires
constrained optimization of only two parameters, eliminating the reliance on initial guess
quality. The BIA, on the other hand, provides the added advantage of uncertainty quantification
for the predicted source locations, enhancing the reliability of the results. In the work presented
here, the effectiveness of the two proposed approaches is investigated first using idealized data,
followed by numerical studies involving models of plates with varying degrees of anisotropy.
Additionally, experimental validation of the approaches is presented. The results show that
both the EEA and BIA are well-suited for practical applications of AE source localization in
anisotropic plates.

with numerous methodologies developed over the years to effectively localize AE sources. For source localizaton in isotropic plates,
a triangulation method based on the time difference of arrival (TDOA) of the AE signals at AE sensors was proposed by Tobias [7]
Source localization in anisotropic plates, however, presents greater challenges due to the varying propagation speeds of elastic
waves in different directions. To address this, Meo et al. [8] proposed an AE source localization technique for anisotropic plates by
estimating wave propagation speeds in various directions. Kundu et al. [9,10] proposed an approach based on solving a system of
non-linear equations using an optimization algorithm for source localization in anisotropic plates. For the same purpose, Nakatan
et al. [11] proposed an improved beamforming method by incorporating the direction-dependent wave speed in the formulation.
All these methods rely on the apriori knowledge of the plate material properties, which is not always readily available. To address
that difficulty, Kundu et al. [12] proposed an AE source localization method using an L-shaped sensor cluster arrangement for
anisotropic plates with unknown material properties. Ciampa et al. [13.14] proposed a source localization technique for anisotropic
plates with unknown material properties by utilizing continuous wavelet transform to estimate the time of arrival (TOA). Later,
Kundu et al. [15] proposed a hybrid technique that uses the source location determined by the method described in [12] as an
initial guess. This guess is then refined by minimizing an objective function to achieve a more accurate prediction. A method based
on a beamforming approach was proposed in Xiao et al. [16]. Jang and Kim [17] enhanced the triangulation method [7] to make
it applicable to anisotropic plates by incorporating neural network training, which takes sensor signal magnitudes as input and
gives the distances between the sensors and the sources as output. However, none of these methods explicitly account for the
deviation between the directions of the wave vector and the group velocity vector when predicting the location of the AE source.
This assumption, while valid and accurate for isotropic homogeneous media, might lead to significant inaccuracies when applied to
complex and highly anisotropic structures [18].

Over the years, several localization methods that explicitly address the different directions of the wave vector and the group
velocity vector have been developed for structures with unknown material properties. Baxter et al. [19] proposed an AE source
localization method for complex structures, where wave propagation paths are non-linear due to the structural complexity, offering
a more accurate approach for such environments. Hensman et al. [20] improved the method reported in [19] by using Gaussian
process (GP) regression. Jones et al. [21] extended the application of GP regression by introducing a Bayesian methodology for AE
source localization in complex structures.
AE source localization techniques that do not rely on straight-line wave propagation, applied for highly anisotropic plates with
unknown material properties have also gained significant attention. Park et al. [18] utilized the L-shaped sensor cluster arrangement
reported in [12] along with a wavefront shape-based approach. analyzing two specific wavefront shapes, namely, rhombus and
ellipse, to localize AE sources in highly anisotropic plates with unknown material properties. In a subsequent study, Sen and
Kundu [22] modified the elliptical wavefront-based approach from [18] to relate the wavefront geometry with the recorded signa
data, and also proposed a more general parametric curve-based approach. The wavefront shape-based techniques proposed in [22]
were enhanced by Sen and Kundu [23]. allowing the modified methods to be applied in situations where the orientation of the axes
of symmetry of the anisotropic plate is not known apriori. Consequently. the methods outlined in [23] represent the most advanced
versions of the wavefront shape-based techniques till date. To offer a better alternative to L-shaped sensor clusters, Sen et al. [24]
explored the use of square-shaped sensor clusters with the wavefront shape-based methods reported in [23]. More recently, Ma
et al. [25] combined the wavefront shape-based source localization technique reported in [23] with the theory of secondary acoustic
source and the baseline technique. This combined approach allows for the active detection and localization of existing damage
in anisotropic plates where the orientation of the axes of symmetry is known. Among the latest versions of the wavefront shape-
based techniques, the ellipse-based method demonstrates slightly better predictive accuracy compared to the parametric curve-based
technique, as it employs one less unknown parameter [23]. However, the current ellipse-based technique requires unconstrained
optimization of four unknown parameters with at least five initial guesses for each. Variations in these initial guesses can lead
to significantly different source location predictions, making the method highly dependent on selecting initial guesses for reliable
results.
In this paper, we propose two source localization techniques, namely, the equation error approach (EEA) and the Bayesian
inference approach (BIA)
, for anisotropic plates with unknown material properties and orientations of the axes of symmetry.
The EEA improves upon the current ellipse-based wavefront method by utilizing constrained optimization of only two parameters,
thereby eliminating the dependence of source location predictions on the quality of the initial guesses. The BIA, on the other
hand, provides source localization within a Bayesian framework, requiring unconstrained optimization of four parameters. However,
unlike the current ellipse-based method, both BIA and EEA need only one initial guess for each parameter. Furthermore, the BIA
provides uncertainty estimates for the source location predictions, thus enhancing the ability to assess the reliability of the predicted
source locations. This capability allows for more informed decision-making in evaluating the accuracy and confidence of AE source
localization results.

BIA are investigated through numerical studies. These studies were performed for 60 plates with varying degrees of anisotropy.

7. Summary and conclusions
In this paper, we proposed two methods, EEA and BIA, for acoustic emission source localization in anisotropic plates where the
orientation of the axes of symmetry and material properties are unknown. The EEA method involves constrained optimization of two
variables, whereas the BIA method requires unconstrained optimization with respect to four variables of the elliptical wavefront.
To investigate the effectiveness of these methods, the source localization was performed using idealized data with varying
numbers of point sensor clusters. The results showed that both EEA and BIA yielded similar predictions under ideal conditions,
accurately identifying the source location when errors in arrival angles were absent. However, in the presence of errors, deviations
